editorial.title: Star ratings get gamed. Source documents don't.
editorial.p1: TrustGive aggregates public registries — IRS Form 990, UK Charity Commission, Минюст СОНКО — and links directly to the source documents. We don't publish a trust score. We don't process payments. The job of the platform is to take you to the original record in one click.

notChecked.title: What we didn't check
notChecked.body: We confirmed that this organisation is registered with its regulator and has filed the accounts linked above. We did not assess how well it spends the money, how much of it reaches the work, or whether it is a good place for your donation. Nothing on this page is a recommendation — a verified badge means a document exists and opens, nothing more.

about.title: About
about.lead: TrustGive is built and run by one person. It takes no money from charities, runs no ads, and has no investors. Here is who I am and what that means for what you're reading.
about.whoBody: I'm Alex Diachenko. I build software, and I live in Moscow. TrustGive started as a weekend question and turned into the thing I work on. There is no team behind it — when this site is wrong, it's my mistake, and when it's fixed, I fixed it.
about.whyBody1: I went to donate and stopped at a question I couldn't answer: who decides which charities are real? The large rating sites publish scores whose method I couldn't follow, and which nonprofits learn to work around — Charity Navigator dropped its overhead-ratio metric in 2023 for that reason. The donation platforms add 10–18% on top of a gift before the charity sees it.
about.whyBody2: So this site doesn't score anything. It finds the filing the regulator holds and links straight to it. You read the document and decide. Donations happen on the charity's own site, not here.
about.moneyBody: It isn't. Infrastructure costs about nothing — a small database, a worker, free public APIs. Charities cannot pay to be listed, to rank higher, or to be removed. There is no revenue to protect, which is the only reason I can afford to delist an organisation the moment its filing stops resolving.
about.limitsBody: Three limits worth knowing before you rely on anything here:
about.limit1: A verified badge means the organisation is registered and has filed. It says nothing about whether the money is spent well. That's a harder question and I don't answer it.
about.limit2: Coverage follows the registers, not the sector. Countries whose regulators publish machine-readable records are represented; countries whose regulators don't are missing, regardless of how good their charities are.
about.limit3: Filings run one to two years behind. That's the regulator's cycle, not a gap in the data.
about.errorBody: Tell me. I've already found four organisations listed under another entity's registration number — one of them filed under the Gates Foundation. I found those by auditing my own data, but I won't catch everything. A specific report with the charity's name gets fixed faster than a general complaint.
about.openBody: The code, the method and the API are public. You don't have to take my word for how verification works — you can read the code that does it, or query the same data directly.

sources.title: Data sources
sources.lead: Everything in the catalogue comes from a public register. This page lists which ones, what each covers, and where each falls short.
sources.howBody: A nightly job re-reads every US filing from ProPublica and re-checks every source link in the catalogue. A charity whose link stops resolving is removed from public view the same night — not flagged, removed. Nothing here is entered by hand except the two-sentence descriptions and the translations.

propublica.name: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer
propublica.meta: United States · Form 990 · free, no key
propublica.body: Mirrors the IRS release of Form 990 filings for US 501(c)(3) organisations. Supplies the registration number, the fiscal period covered, total revenue and executive compensation. This is the largest single source in the catalogue.
propublica.limit: Filings appear one to two years after the fiscal year ends, and the API returns nothing for organisations that file on paper or fall below the electronic filing threshold.

charityCommission.name: Charity Commission for England and Wales
charityCommission.body: The statutory register of charities in England and Wales, with accounts and annual returns filed against each registration number.
charityCommission.limit: Covers England and Wales only. Scottish and Northern Irish charities sit under separate regulators that are not yet integrated here.

acnc.name: Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission
acnc.body: The national charity register, matched to the Australian Business Register record for each organisation.
acnc.limit: The register does not expose per-charity revenue, so Australian entries carry a verified registration without a money breakdown. Several national bodies share a domain with their state branches, which makes automatic matching unreliable — those are resolved by hand or left out.

minjust.name: Минюст СОНКО
minjust.body: The Ministry of Justice register of socially oriented non-profit organisations, used for the small curated Russian selection.
minjust.limit: Registration confirms legal existence and nothing else. Russian entries are curated rather than loaded in bulk, and the legal exclusions described in the methodology apply.

sources.missingBody: Coverage follows what regulators publish, not what matters. Two absences are worth naming:
sources.missingCanada: Canada. The CRA charity register has no stable public address for an individual charity — the URL that looks like one returns an identical page for every input, including invented registration numbers, and an error in a browser. There is no document to link to, so no Canadian charity is published here.
sources.missingEurope: Most of continental Europe. Charity registers are national and heterogeneous; many publish no machine-readable per-organisation record, and smaller organisations file only on paper.
sources.useBody: The same records the site reads are available from the public API, unauthenticated. If you are citing the catalogue in research, query it directly rather than scraping the pages — and note the date, because entries are removed when their evidence stops resolving.

methodology.title: How we verify
methodology.lead: We don't grade charities. We show you the documents that grade them for us — and link straight to those documents.
methodology.verifiedMeansBody: A charity is marked Verified on TrustGive if all three are true: (1) it is registered with at least one government registry; (2) it has filed financial documents in the last 24 months; (3) we link directly to those documents on the charity's page.
methodology.catalogueTitle: Why this catalogue is smaller than it could be
methodology.catalogueBody: Every organisation listed here has a regulator filing you can open in one click. If we cannot confirm that document, the organisation does not appear at all — we don't publish it with a caveat, a lower rating, or an "unverified" label. A directory that mixes confirmed and unconfirmed entries quietly transfers the checking work back to you, which defeats the purpose.
methodology.catalogueBody2: This has a cost we'd rather state than hide: real, reputable charities are missing from these pages. Some national registers publish no per-organisation record we can link to, and some organisations file only on paper. Their absence is a limitation of what we can prove, not a judgement about them. If a charity you trust isn't here, that is the most likely reason.
methodology.doNotVerifyBody: We do not assess program effectiveness, mission outcomes, or donor satisfaction. For deeper rigor, we recommend GiveWell, Effektiv-Spenden, and CharityWatch.
methodology.complianceBody: TrustGive is operated from Russia. Russian law requires us to exclude the following categories of organisations from our catalogue, regardless of the work they do:
methodology.complianceItem1: Organisations recognised as foreign agents by the Ministry of Justice of the Russian Federation
methodology.complianceItem2: Organisations recognised as extremist or undesirable by Russian courts or executive bodies
methodology.complianceItem3: Organisations providing material assistance to parties of active armed conflicts
methodology.complianceItem4: Organisations registered in territories where compliance with Russian regulations cannot be reliably verified
methodology.complianceFooter: These exclusions are a legal compliance requirement, not an editorial judgement about the work these organisations do. Donors who wish to support such organisations can do so directly through other discovery tools.
methodology.deeperBody: For mission-effectiveness analysis, we recommend GiveWell, Effektiv-Spenden, and CharityWatch.
